passages.t: Heaven and earth called to witness
passages.happening:
‘This is the vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem that Isaiah son of Amoz saw during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah’ (verse 1).

Then the LORD calls the heavens and the earth to listen: ‘I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me’ (verse 2). Even an ox knows its owner, and a donkey knows where its master feeds it, ‘but Israel does not know; My people do not understand’ (verse 3).

The nation is weighed down with guilt. They have forsaken the LORD and ‘despised the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 4). Why do they want more beatings? From head to foot there is no soundness, only wounds and sores no one has bandaged (verses 5-6). The land is desolate, the cities burned, and foreigners eat the fields (verse 7). Jerusalem is left alone ‘like a shelter in a vineyard, like a shack in a cucumber field, like a city besieged’ (verse 8).

‘Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, we would have become like Sodom’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The heading places Isaiah's work in the reigns of four kings of Judah, spanning roughly the second half of the eighth century BC and the start of the seventh. Uzziah's long reign had been prosperous, but prosperity bred complacency and injustice, the same sins Isaiah's contemporaries Amos and Micah denounced. Meanwhile Assyria was pushing west toward Judah.

The chapter opens like a courtroom. Ancient treaties between kings and their vassals called gods and the powers of the world as witnesses, and Israel's covenant had heaven and earth as its witnesses. When Isaiah calls them to listen, the first hearers knew that the covenant's terms were being enforced.

The charge is personal. The word for rebel, pasha, was used for a vassal breaking faith with his overlord. God speaks as a father whose children turned on him.

Verses 7 and 8 describe a land burned and occupied, with Jerusalem left alone. Many scholars connect this with Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC, when his annals boast of taking forty-six of Hezekiah's walled towns. If so, the chapter may come from late in Isaiah's ministry and was placed first because it gathers up his message. Others connect it with the attack by Aram and Israel around 735 BC. The chapter does not say. Many scholars see it as an overture to the whole book.
passages.later: Moses' song begins the same way: ‘Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; hear, O earth, the words of my mouth’ (Deuteronomy 32:1). Paul quotes verse 9 to show that God has always kept a remnant: ‘Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom’ (Romans 9:29).
passages.asks: God says even an ox knows its owner, but his people do not know him. Ask whether you know who feeds you, and whether you live like it. And ask where you keep wanting more beatings rather than turning back.

passages.t: Worship God refuses, and the justice he requires
passages.happening:
‘Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom’ (verse 10). Isaiah turns the comparison on Jerusalem's leaders.

The LORD asks what good their many sacrifices are to him. He is full of burnt offerings and takes no delight in the blood of bulls and lambs and goats (verse 11). Who asked them to trample his courts (verse 12)? ‘Bring your worthless offerings no more’ (verse 13). He cannot bear their New Moons, Sabbaths and feasts with iniquity in them. ‘I hate your New Moons and your appointed feasts’ (verse 14).

‘When you spread out your hands in prayer, I will hide My eyes from you; even though you multiply your prayers, I will not listen. Your hands are covered with blood’ (verse 15).

Then the call: ‘Wash and cleanse yourselves’ (verse 16). Stop doing evil. ‘Learn to do right; seek justice and correct the oppressor. Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The worship Isaiah describes was the lawful worship of the temple: burnt offerings, New Moons (the monthly festival), Sabbaths and appointed feasts. God had commanded them. The problem was not the rituals. It was that they were offered by people whose hands were covered with blood and who ignored the fatherless and the widow.

In Israel's law, orphans and widows were the classic examples of people without a protector or an advocate in court, and God repeatedly names himself as their defender. Justice, mishpat, means the right ordering of a community, especially fair judgment for those who cannot defend themselves.

The first hearers thought their worship was keeping them safe. Isaiah told them God would not even look at it. The prophet is not against worship. He is against worship cut off from obedience, worship that treats God as a patron to be paid while the poor are crushed.
passages.later: Samuel had said the same to Saul: ‘obedience is better than sacrifice’ (1 Samuel 15:22). Amos cried, ‘let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream’ (Amos 5:24). And Micah asked, ‘what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?’ (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard:
Did God reject the sacrifices he himself commanded?

Verses 11 to 15 sound as though God hates the whole system of worship he gave in Leviticus. Some older critical scholars took passages like this, with Amos 5 and Hosea 6, as evidence that the prophets opposed ritual altogether. Most interpreters today read it differently. The key line is verse 15: God will not listen because their hands are covered with blood. The Hebrew Bible often uses this kind of absolute contrast to express priority, as when Samuel says obedience is better than sacrifice.

Worship that treats God as someone to be paid off while the weak are crushed is not worship of the God of Israel at all. The same book that condemns these offerings later calls God's house ‘a house of prayer for all the nations’ (56:7).
passages.asks: God refused the prayers of people whose hands were covered with blood. Ask whether there is anything in your life that makes your worship hollow. And ask who are the fatherless and the widows near you, and whether anyone pleads their case.

passages.happening:
Then comes the surprise. ‘Come now, let us reason together,’ says the LORD (verse 18). ‘Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool’ (verse 18).

But there is a choice. ‘If you are willing and obedient, you will eat the best of the land’ (verse 19). ‘But if you resist and rebel, you will be devoured by the sword’ (verse 20). ‘For the mouth of the LORD has spoken’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The word translated reason together, yakach, is a legal word: to settle a case in court. God is not inviting a casual chat. He is calling the accused to face the verdict, and then he surprises them with an offer of cleansing.

Scarlet and crimson were deep, lasting dyes, hard to wash out. The first hearers, whose hands were covered with blood, are told that God can make what is stained red as white as snow and wool.

The offer is real, and so is the choice. Obedience leads to eating the best of the land. Rebellion leads to the sword. The covenant's promises and curses stand behind both.
passages.later: David prayed for the same cleansing: ‘wash me, and I will be whiter than snow’ (Psalm 51:7). Micah says of God, ‘You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea’ (Micah 7:19).
passages.asks: God's offer comes in the middle of the courtroom, after the charge. Ask whether you believe God's mercy is meant for you while you are still guilty. And ask what it would mean to be willing and obedient today.

passages.t: The faithful city corrupted, and promised a new name
passages.happening:
“See how the faithful city has become a harlot! She once was full of justice; righteousness resided within her, but now only murderers!” (verse 21). Her silver has become dross, and her wine is watered down (verse 22). ‘Your rulers are rebels, friends of thieves’ (verse 23). They love bribes, and they do not defend the fatherless or hear the widow's case.

So the Lord GOD of Hosts will turn his hand against the city and purge its dross (verses 24-25). ‘I will restore your judges as at first, and your counselors as at the beginning. After that you will be called the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City’ (verse 26).

‘Zion will be redeemed with justice, her repentant ones with righteousness’ (verse 27). But rebels and sinners will be broken together, and those who forsake the LORD will perish (verse 28). They will be ashamed of the sacred oaks and gardens they chose (verse 29), and become like a withered oak and a garden without water (verse 30). ‘The strong man will become tinder and his work will be a spark; both will burn together, with no one to quench the flames’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Verses 21 to 26 form a ring. The city that was faithful and full of justice will again be called the Faithful City. In between, God promises to refine her as silver is refined, by melting away the dross. Judgment here is not only destruction. It is purifying.

The charge against the rulers is specific: bribes, and no justice for the weak. The first hearers knew who sat in the city's courts.

The sacred oaks and gardens of verse 29 were places of fertility worship borrowed from Canaanite religion. Those who trusted them will become like a dead oak and a dry garden. The chapter ends with fire, a picture of judgment that consumes the strong man and his works together. The book's last chapter returns to the same pictures of gardens and fire.

The prophets often spoke of a city as a woman, and of its unfaithfulness as a wife's. In this verse the harlot is Jerusalem, and her sin is murder, bribery and injustice. It is a picture of a city. It gives no one leave to shame or to harm a woman.
passages.later: Isaiah later promises that the same Zion will receive a new name: ‘No longer will you be called Forsaken’ (Isaiah 62:4). Micah charges Jerusalem's leaders in the same way, saying they ‘build Zion with bloodshed’ (Micah 3:10).
passages.asks: God promises to purge the city's dross and give it back its old name. Ask what dross in your own life God might be burning away. And ask whether the leaders you have any say over defend the fatherless, or love rewards.
